extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers and anyone seeking an overview of controversies involving Uber
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and communicate corporate controversies, legal exposures, regulatory conflicts, privacy incidents, workplace misconduct, and reputational risks arising from a company's actions; useful for crisis communications, media backgrounders, and stakeholder briefings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring and evading local regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Uber has been criticized for generally commencing operations in a city without regard for local regulations and for mounting political and lobbying campaigns when faced with regulatory opposition; the company argued it was a 'technology company' not a taxi company and followed a strategy to 'seek forgiveness rather than permission'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include paying citations for drivers, public opinion campaigns (e.g., California AB5 response), and leaked documents showing coordinated lobbying. For communications: explain the business rationale, legal exposure, any remediation, and cite specific incidents or leaked evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal action from taxi companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxi companies sued Uber alleging unfair competition or antitrust violations arising from Uber's policy of violating taxi regulations; some courts found intentional violations but Uber prevailed in many cases; settlements include a $178 million payout in Australia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing legal disputes, include jurisdiction, claims (unfair competition, antitrust), outcomes (trial rulings, settlements), and financial or operational impacts on affected parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greyball (use of software to evade authorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uber developed a software tool called 'Greyball' to avoid giving rides to known law enforcement officers in areas where its service was illegal, identifying officials via geofencing, credit card data, device IDs and social media; Uber later admitted use to skirt regulations and promised to stop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the technical methods alleged, jurisdictions where it was used (e.g., Portland, Australia, South Korea, China, multiple European countries), internal knowledge of senior management, investigations by authorities, and any regulator responses such as licence decisions (Transport for London).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill switch (blocking access during raids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uber routinely used a 'kill switch' (codenamed 'Ripley') to lock, power off and change passwords on staff computers during government raids to prevent authorities accessing data; used in multiple countries and confirmed in reporting and leaked documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe frequency and contexts of use, the company's stated justifications (protecting IP, customer privacy), investigations or fines (e.g., employee fined in the Netherlands), and whether data was later made available to authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempts to sabotage competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that Uber employees ordered and cancelled rides on competing services (Lyft, Gett) to disrupt them and recruited users/drivers from competitors; Uber denied involvement in some accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List specific tactics alleged (fake orders, targeted recruitment), evidence (internal documents, counts of cancelled rides), company responses, and any quantified impact reported by competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage disputes and misleading driver earnings claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and legal actions that Uber misled drivers about potential earnings and underpaid drivers (e.g., FTC $20 million settlement; class actions over fare policies; admitted underpaying NYC drivers by tens of millions), with various settlements and judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include regulatory or litigation outcomes, class-action settlements and amounts, nature of the misleading claims, and corrective steps or policy changes by the company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boycotts and public backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer boycotts (e.g., #DeleteUber) arose from perceived political affiliations or company actions; large numbers of users deleted the app and executives resigned from advisory councils amid backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting, mention catalysts (specific political events or executive actions), scale of user response, reputational impact, and executive or policy changes that followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual assault incidents reported by passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting that Uber received reports of sexual assault or sexual misconduct at high frequency (claimed in later reporting to be almost every eight minutes in a given period), indicating serious passenger-safety concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timeframes, data sources (investigations, media reports), company reporting procedures, victim support measures, and reforms or settlements related to safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual harassment and workplace culture
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile allegations of sexual harassment (e.g., Susan Fowler's account), nondisclosure of past claims by executives, internal investigations (led by external investigators), firings of employees, and leadership changes including CEO resignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document whistleblower accounts, investigation findings, disciplinary actions, settlements (e.g., $7 million gender discrimination/harassment settlement), and steps taken to change culture and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: God View and privacy concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about an internal 'God View' tool allowing employee tracking of specific customers' whereabouts; congressional inquiries led to Uber restricting the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain what capabilities were available, oversight or misuse incidents (tracking journalists/politicians), regulatory scrutiny, and changes to internal access controls and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed disclosure of data breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Uber admitted to delaying disclosure of data breaches (e.g., a 2014 breach disclosed months later; a 2016 breach exposing millions disclosed in 2017), including allegations of paying hackers to delete stolen data and concealing breaches from authorities and users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List scale and types of data exposed, timelines of discovery versus disclosure, law enforcement or regulatory findings (FTC, ICO fines, multi-state settlements, criminal charges), and remediation or notification practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax avoidance/tax evasion allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Revelations from the Paradise Papers that Uber used offshore structures to minimize taxes and moved executives to influence tax residency claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the offshore structures alleged, implicated jurisdictions, public and regulatory responses, and any corporate governance or tax-policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drivers' employment status and worker classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal rulings and tribunals (e.g., UK Employment Tribunal) found drivers were 'workers' rather than self-employed, affording rights like paid annual leave and national minimum wage, with broad implications for labor classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference specific legal decisions, the rights conferred, jurisdictional differences, and consequences for pay, benefits, and company operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination against disabled customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases such as a blind customer with a guide dog being denied rides resulting in large damages awards (e.g., $1.1 million), highlighting failure to accommodate disabled passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include incident summaries, legal/arbitration outcomes, amounts awarded, and policies or training changes to address access and accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated 'robo-firings' and GDPR Article 22 issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A court (Amsterdam) ruled Uber must reinstate and compensate drivers allegedly terminated solely by algorithmic decisions, citing GDPR protections against automated decisions causing legal/significant impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the legal basis (GDPR Article 22), the nature of algorithmic decision-making at issue, company defenses, and implications for automated personnel systems and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racial discrimination and biased rating/algorithm systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Class actions and suits alleged racial discrimination in how passenger ratings and facial-recognition algorithms were used, with claims that these systems disproportionately harmed non-White drivers and people of color; some suits were dismissed but allowed to be refiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report alleged mechanisms of bias (customer ratings, algorithmic ID failures), jurisdictions and outcomes, technical audit findings if any, and mitigation steps (algorithmic fairness reviews, policy changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger safety incidents and regulatory consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents of passenger assault (e.g., New Delhi assault) triggered withdrawals, local operational changes, and criticisms about missing or non-functioning mandated safety features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide incident details, regulatory responses (suspensions, mandates for panic buttons), company actions to restore service, and measures to improve passenger safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Driver safety and working conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents and reporting claim Uber created working conditions that left drivers scraping by and incentivised risky routes/schedules, sometimes exposing them to violence; internal memos suggested tolerating risk for business goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include studies, leaked documents, driver testimony, any policy or remuneration reforms, and safety programs aimed at protecting drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration agreements and class action waivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Uber's arbitration clauses and class action waivers in terms of service have been challenged; courts (e.g., Pennsylvania Superior Court) found procedural/constitutional issues with how waivers were presented and enforced, impacting enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the contractual language, procedural notice requirements (e.g., conspicuous bold text in Pennsylvania), key appellate rulings, and the effects on consumer/worker access to court remedies.
